title: Serve the site from one production HTTPS origin
statement: Exactly one scheme-and-host pair serves public content. Every other host or scheme that resolves for the site issues a permanent redirect to that origin rather than serving a second copy of the same pages.
rationale: When more than one origin serves the same pages, every URL exists more than once, external link signals are split across the copies, and the search engine rather than the site decides which origin represents the content.
implementation: Find where the deployment terminates TLS and resolves hostnames, declare the chosen origin once in configuration, and redirect the remaining hostnames and the http scheme to it with 301. Do not add application-level redirects if the hosting platform already owns hostname routing.

verification.method: Request each hostname and scheme that resolves for the site and record the full redirect chain and final URL for every one of them.

sources.title: How to specify a canonical URL with rel="canonical" and other methods

title: Return an accurate HTTP status code for every public route state
statement: Each public route state resolves to the status code that describes it: success, permanent move, temporary move, missing, gone, unauthorized, or server error. No failure or empty state responds with 200.
rationale: Crawlers act on the status line rather than on the page text, so a 200 on a failure page keeps a dead URL in the index, hides the fault from crawl-error reporting, and can add the error template to the set of indexable content.
implementation: Enumerate the route states the application can produce, then trace each one to the status it actually returns. Set the status at the layer that owns the response - framework route handler, error boundary, or middleware - and keep the status assignment next to the state that causes it rather than in a catch-all handler.

verification.method: Request one URL per route state, including a deliberately missing path and a deliberately unauthorized path, and record the status line returned for each.

title: Prevent query-parameter variants from creating crawlable duplicates
statement: URLs that differ from a canonical URL only by tracking, session, or result-ordering parameters are not linked internally, are absent from the sitemap, and declare the parameter-free URL as their canonical.
rationale: Parameter permutations multiply the crawlable URL set without adding content, so crawl capacity is spent refetching copies of pages that are already indexed under their clean URL.
implementation: List the query parameters the application reads and classify each one as content-defining or presentational. Strip presentational and tracking parameters when building internal links, canonical values, and sitemap entries; leave the parameters working on inbound requests so shared links keep functioning.

verification.method: Request a canonical URL with tracking and ordering parameters appended and confirm the response declares the parameter-free URL as canonical.

sources.title: Large site owner's guide to managing your crawl budget

title: Enforce a single trailing-slash form per path
statement: For every public path, one of the slash-terminated and non-slash-terminated forms serves the content and the other returns a permanent redirect to it. Both forms never return 200 for the same resource.
rationale: Two forms of the same path both answering with content produce a duplicate for every page on the site, which halves the link signal reaching each one and doubles the number of URLs a crawler has to fetch.
implementation: Determine which form the framework or host already emits by default and adopt it rather than fighting it. Configure the single normalization rule at the routing or edge layer, then confirm internal links, the sitemap, and canonical values all use the chosen form.

verification.method: Request a representative path in both slash forms and record which one returns content and which one redirects, with the status code.

title: Preserve inbound URLs across migrations with a permanent redirect map
statement: Every URL that was publicly reachable before a structural change either still resolves or redirects permanently to its closest live equivalent, and the mapping is stored in the repository rather than only in a platform console.
rationale: An unmapped URL loses the external links pointing at it and the index has to rediscover the new structure from scratch, so traffic to the old address is discarded rather than transferred.
implementation: Capture the old URL inventory from the sitemap, route manifest, or server logs before changing routes. Express the mapping as data in the repository, mapping each retired URL to one live target, and use 410 only where no equivalent exists. Never map a large set of unrelated URLs onto the home page.

verification.method: Sample the retired URL inventory, request each sampled URL, and record the status, redirect target, and whether the target returns content.

title: Resolve every redirect in one hop without loops
statement: No public URL needs more than one redirect to reach the response that serves content, and no redirect sequence returns to a URL it has already visited.
rationale: Each extra hop is an additional round trip that a crawler may abandon before reaching the destination, and a loop makes the target unreachable for crawlers and browsers alike.
implementation: Collect the redirect rules from every layer that can emit one - edge configuration, middleware, framework routing, and application handlers - and compose them to find sequences longer than one hop. Collapse each sequence by pointing the first rule directly at the final target.

verification.method: Request each URL known to redirect without following automatically, then follow one hop at a time and record the resulting chain length.

title: Return 404 or 410 for removed resources instead of an empty 200 page
statement: A URL whose resource no longer exists responds 404 or 410. It does not respond 200 with an empty template, a search prompt, or a redirect to an unrelated landing page.
rationale: A success response on a removed URL is a soft 404: the URL stays in the index competing with live pages, and the removal never propagates because nothing in the response reports that the resource is gone.
implementation: Trace the not-found path of each dynamic route and make the handler set the status rather than rendering a placeholder. Use 410 when the removal is deliberate and permanent, 404 otherwise, and keep the human-readable page body while the status stays correct.

verification.method: Request a path that matches a dynamic route pattern but has no backing resource and record the status code alongside the response body.
